avoid.reason: Crime is minimal, but mind crush-level crowds in Gion and Higashiyama and note that photography is banned (with fines) on Gion's private alleys.

hood_desc: Gion is Kyoto's famous geisha district of wooden teahouses, lantern-lit lanes and traditional performances, ideal for travelers seeking classic old-Japan atmosphere and culture.
Higashiyama is the beautifully preserved eastern temple district around Kiyomizu-dera and Sannenzaka, full of shrines and craft shops, perfect for sightseeing and history lovers.
Arashiyama is a scenic western area of bamboo groves, riverside walks, temples and monkey park, a nature-focused, day-trip-style base great for photographers and families.
Pontocho is a narrow, atmospheric alley beside the Kamo River lined with intimate restaurants and bars, ideal for evening dining, romance and traditional nightlife.
Fushimi is the sake-brewing southern district and home of Fushimi Inari's thousand torii gates, appealing to travelers wanting shrines, sake tasting and fewer crowds.

water.note: Tap water is treated to a high standard and safe to drink anywhere.

transit.pay: Use a rechargeable IC card — ICOCA locally, or Suica/Pasmo from elsewhere in Japan (500 JPY deposit, ~US$3.50) — bought at station ticket machines; tap on the subway, trains and buses. City buses are a flat 230 JPY, paid (or tapped) as you exit. The subway + bus one-day pass (1,100 JPY, ~US$7) from station machines is great value on busy sightseeing days.
transit.hours: The subway runs about 5:30am-11:30pm; city buses run roughly 6am-10pm with no night service.

landmarks: Kiyomizu-dera
A magnificent wooden temple built on a hillside without nails, its huge veranda offers sweeping views over Kyoto and cherry/maple trees.
Fushimi Inari Taisha
Famous for its thousands of vermilion torii gates winding up the mountainside, one of the most photographed sights in Japan.
Kinkaku-ji (Golden Pavilion)
A stunning gold-leaf-covered Zen temple perfectly mirrored in its surrounding pond, an unmistakable icon of Kyoto.
Ginkaku-ji (Silver Pavilion)
An elegant temple with meticulously raked sand gardens and a moss garden, quieter and more understated than its golden counterpart.
Arashiyama Bamboo Grove
A towering, otherworldly bamboo forest path on Kyoto's western edge, one of the most surreal and photogenic natural spots in Japan.
Ryōan-ji
Home to Japan's most famous kare-sansui (dry rock garden), a minimalist arrangement of 15 stones in raked gravel.
Nijō Castle
A UNESCO-listed shogun's castle famous for its ornate Ninomaru Palace and 'nightingale floors' that chirp to detect intruders.
Kyoto Imperial Palace
The former residence of Japan's Imperial family, set within vast traditional gardens and stately Heian-era architecture.
Gion (Yasaka Shrine area)
Kyoto's famed geisha district, with lantern-lit streets, traditional teahouses, and the vermilion Yasaka Shrine at its entrance.
Kyoto Tower
A sleek white observation tower resembling a lit candle, offering panoramic night views over the historic city.

train.note: Japan is an island nation with no international trains. Kyoto Station is a major stop on the Tokaido Shinkansen (Tokyo about 2 hours 15 minutes, Shin-Osaka about 15 minutes) - book online with the official SmartEX service, while JR West's e5489 covers the Thunderbird, Kinosaki and other limited expresses. Private railways add useful options: the Kintetsu line runs to Nara and the Keihan and Hankyu lines to Osaka, all cheaper than JR. Reserved Shinkansen seats open 1 month ahead and sell out around Golden Week and the autumn leaves.

bus.note: No international buses exist from Japan. Long-distance highway and overnight buses are run by operators such as Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) and JR Bus, mostly from the Hachijo exit on the south side of Kyoto Station. Overnight coaches to Tokyo take about 8 hours and cost a fraction of the Shinkansen fare; seats are booked online in English with Willer or at the station counter.

intl.to: Busan (South Korea) - sails from Osaka, not Kyoto

ferry.note: Kyoto is inland and has no port of its own. The nearest international sailing is the Panstar overnight cruise ferry from Osaka Port, about an hour away by train, to Busan, with several departures a week. For domestic boats you would go to Kobe or Osaka; the Japan Sea coast at Maizuru, about 2 hours north, has long-haul ferries to Hokkaido.
